name: Cambodian chapei dang veng
lineage: Cambodian chapei dang veng narrative-and-improvisatory song tradition. The chapei (two-string long-neck fretted plucked lute) accompanies a single male singer-performer who alternates between strophic-narrative verse passages (drawing on Khmer historical-epic, Reamker / Ramayana, and contemporary-social-commentary repertoires) and improvised satirical-and-praise-poetry verses that respond to the present audience and occasion. The form is genealogically connected to broader Southeast-Asian narrative-poet traditions (the Lao mor lam genealogically adjacent, the Thai mor lam-thai also related) and to the Indic-derived bardic-poet lineages that traveled along the Theravada Buddhist transmission routes. Performance contexts span village wedding feasts, temple-festival night entertainments, and the post-1980 revival concert circuit. The Khmer Rouge era 1975-1979 nearly extinguished the tradition (only a handful of master practitioners survived); the post-1980 revival has been driven by master Kong Nay (born 1944, blind from childhood, the canonical twentieth-century chapei singer) and his students under the Cambodian Living Arts foundation. Modal vocabulary draws on the seven-equal-tempered tuning shared with broader Khmer classical traditions. Distinguished from pinpeat by chapei's solo-narrative-with-lute (vs court-ensemble) configuration; distinguished from Lao mor lam by Khmer-language repertoire and chapei (vs khaen mouth-organ) instrumental accompaniment; distinguished from Cambodian smot Buddhist-chant by chapei's secular-narrative (vs liturgical) functional context.
